title: Dimension reduction: rank, SVD, and CUR
summary: Use Lecture 4 to reduce a high-dimensional matrix with SVD, select rank from reconstruction error, and compare the dense latent representation with sparse, interpretable CUR.
objectives: Relate effective rank and maximum-variance projection to low-dimensional representation
Read the roles, shapes, and constraints of U, Sigma, and V in SVD
Compute projection coordinates, retained energy, and rank-k Frobenius error
Explain power iteration and the A-transpose-A eigenvector connection
Choose between SVD and CUR using accuracy, sparsity, runtime, and interpretability

sourceLens.whyExaminable: The supplied Lecture 4 is the official local source for rank, SVD, low-rank error, power iteration, concept-space queries, and CUR. Stanford CS246 and MMDS are supporting depth only.

sections.title: Reduce effective dimension, not meaning
sections.body: A high-dimensional matrix can have a much smaller effective rank. Dimension reduction searches for a few directions that capture the greatest variance, equivalently minimizing projection or reconstruction error. Start by naming the original rows, columns, and the downstream quantity that must survive.

sections.title: Read the SVD factors by shape
sections.body: The truncated SVD writes $A\approx U\Sigma V^T$. $U$ maps rows to latent concepts, $V$ maps columns to latent concepts, and $\Sigma$ weights the concepts by non-negative singular values. The columns of $U$ and $V$ are orthonormal, so the factors are constrained rather than arbitrary.

sections.title: Project, reconstruct, and choose rank
sections.body: Projection uses the leading right singular directions, while reconstruction keeps only the largest singular values. For the best rank-$k$ approximation, the squared Frobenius error is the squared energy in the discarded tail. Increasing $k$ reduces error but keeps more dimensions and computation.

sections.title: Compute directions through eigenvectors
sections.body: Power iteration normalizes repeated multiplication by a symmetric matrix to approach its principal eigenvector. From $A=U\Sigma V^T$, we obtain $A^TA=V\Sigma^2V^T$, so the eigenvectors of $A^TA$ are the right singular vectors and its eigenvalues are squared singular values. Deflation exposes later directions.

sections.title: Query in one concept space
sections.body: SVD also changes retrieval: map a query and stored objects into the same latent coordinates, for example $q_{concept}=qV$. Two objects can then be similar because they share latent concepts even when they have no exact non-zero entry in the original sparse matrix.

sections.title: Use CUR when actual rows and columns matter
sections.body: CUR approximates $A$ with sampled columns $C$, sampled rows $R$, and an intersection factor $U$. The sampled basis can remain sparse and interpretable, but randomized sampling can duplicate rows or columns and does not inherit SVD's optimal low-rank guarantee. Compare accuracy, space, runtime, and interpretability together.

math.name: Truncated SVD
math.purpose: Represent a matrix using a small number of latent directions.
math.explanation: The product $A\approx U\Sigma V^T$ uses $U$ and $V$ for orthonormal directions and $\Sigma$ for their strengths.

math.name: Rank-k reconstruction error
math.purpose: Compute the best rank-k approximation error from the discarded singular values.
math.explanation: The squared Frobenius reconstruction error $\lVert A-A_k\rVert_F^2$ is the squared energy of singular directions removed after the rank-$k$ cutoff.

symbols.meaning: i-th singular value in descending order

math.name: Power iteration
math.purpose: Approximate the principal eigenvector of a symmetric matrix.
math.explanation: Power iteration repeatedly applies $M$ and normalizes the result; for $M=A^TA$, the leading direction is a right singular vector of $A$.

math.name: CUR approximation
math.purpose: Approximate a matrix with sampled original rows and columns.
math.explanation: CUR keeps actual sampled columns $C$ and rows $R$ and uses $U$ from their intersection to form a compact approximation.

algorithmNotes.problemDefinition: Replace a high-dimensional matrix with a rank-k representation that preserves the most useful variation while minimizing reconstruction error.
algorithmNotes.assumptions: The input matrix and Frobenius reconstruction loss are appropriate, singular values are ordered, and k is chosen from an explicit accuracy or resource target.
algorithmNotes.coreInvariant: The leading singular directions give the best rank-k approximation in Frobenius norm, and increasing k cannot increase the discarded tail energy.
algorithmNotes.formulaAlgorithm: Compute $A\approx U\Sigma V^T$, retain the first k singular directions, project with $V$, and reconstruct from $U_k\Sigma_kV_k^T$.
algorithmNotes.failureModes: Common mistakes: confusing $A^TA$ eigenvalues with singular values, summing retained rather than discarded energy, treating convergence as global semantic correctness, or ignoring the dense and less interpretable factors.

algorithmNotes.problemDefinition: Recover a dominant eigenvector and eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix as a building block for SVD computation.
algorithmNotes.assumptions: The starting vector has a non-zero component along the dominant eigenvector, the matrix is symmetric, and the dominant direction is sufficiently separated for convergence.
algorithmNotes.coreInvariant: Each iterate is normalized after multiplication, so its direction is amplified toward the largest-eigenvalue component without unbounded scale growth.
algorithmNotes.formulaAlgorithm: Initialize a random $x_0$, repeat $x_{t+1}=Mx_t/\lVert Mx_t\rVert_2$, estimate $\lambda=x^TMx$ after normalization, then deflate before finding later directions.
algorithmNotes.failureModes: Common mistakes: skipping normalization, iterating on the wrong matrix for the requested side, using $\lambda_i$ as $\sigma_i$ without a square root, or forgetting deflation for subsequent vectors.

algorithmNotes.problemDefinition: Build a compact matrix approximation from actual sampled columns and rows when sparsity or interpretability matters.
algorithmNotes.assumptions: Rows and columns can be sampled according to squared-norm importance, duplicate samples are handled deliberately, and an approximation with a stated probability/error contract is acceptable.
algorithmNotes.coreInvariant: C and R remain original matrix columns and rows; U is computed from their intersection, so the representation stays tied to observed data rather than invented dense directions.
algorithmNotes.formulaAlgorithm: Sample columns C and rows R with probability proportional to squared Frobenius norm, form their intersection W, compute its pseudoinverse U=W^+, and use $A\approx CUR$.
algorithmNotes.failureModes: Common mistakes: claiming CUR is the exact SVD, ignoring duplicate rows or columns, sampling uniformly when importance sampling is required, or quoting an error bound without its sample-size and probability conditions.

contrastDrills.pair: eigenvalue of A^T A vs singular value
contrastDrills.prompt: If an eigenvalue of $A^TA$ is $49$, what is the corresponding singular value?
choices: The value of the matching entry of U
It cannot be determined because A is rectangular
contrastDrills.explanation: The eigenvalue is $\sigma_i^2$, so the non-negative singular value is $\sigma_i=\sqrt{49}=7$.
contrastDrills.misconception: Treating the eigenvalue of $A^TA$ as the singular value without taking the non-negative square root.
contrastDrills.repair: Label the number as an entry of $\Sigma^2$ first, then take its square root to recover $\Sigma$.

contrastDrills.prompt: For a rank-$k$ approximation, which singular values belong in the squared Frobenius reconstruction error?
choices: The number of rows times the number of columns
contrastDrills.explanation: The best rank-$k$ error is $\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2$, so only discarded singular directions contribute.
contrastDrills.misconception: Summing retained energy when the question asks for discarded reconstruction error.
contrastDrills.repair: Draw the rank cutoff after $\sigma_k$ and square only the values on the right.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which requirement most strongly favors CUR over SVD?
choices: The basis must remain actual rows and columns from the input
The approximation must be optimal in Frobenius norm
The singular directions must be orthogonal
The data must have no sparse entries
The cluster count must be fixed
contrastDrills.explanation: CUR uses sampled original rows and columns, while SVD uses latent singular directions and is the optimal low-rank approximation under the stated norm.
contrastDrills.misconception: Assuming the two decompositions have the same basis semantics because both use three factors.
contrastDrills.repair: Underline whether the task values optimal latent directions or interpretability as observed rows and columns.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why can dropping a small singular value change less than one percent of reconstruction energy but still change a downstream query?
criticalQuestions.angle: Separate global Frobenius error from task-specific sensitivity to a latent direction.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Frobenius energy is a global aggregate, while a query may depend strongly on the dropped direction. A small global contribution does not prove that every downstream decision is unchanged.

criticalQuestions.prompt: When is CUR a better engineering choice even if SVD has lower reconstruction error?
criticalQuestions.angle: Compare the objective with sparsity, interpretability, memory, and runtime constraints.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: CUR can be preferable when the output must be explained as actual rows and columns or remain sparse and compact, even if it sacrifices some approximation optimality.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What must be checked before using a power-iteration eigenvalue as a singular value?
criticalQuestions.angle: Trace the matrix, side of the factorization, normalization, and square-root step.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Confirm that the eigenvalue came from $A^TA$ or $AA^T$ for the requested singular side, then take its non-negative square root because the eigenvalue equals $\sigma_i^2$.
